title: Lojong Teaching 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness, bodhicitta, and self-awareness in daily life. By recognizing the impermanence of experiences and the interconnectedness of all things, we can develop a more compassionate and intelligent approach to reality. This involves taking responsibility for our actions, trusting our own intelligence, and embracing qualities like humility, humor, and self-trust, which allow us to navigate challenging situations with greater ease and wisdom.

Bodhicitta.

Regard all dharmas as dreams.

That when we take things so literally, so rigidly to be solidly and sort of permanently true our own tendencies, our situation when we feel so hemmed in and trapped, we're probably not seeing all dharmas, meaning all existence, as a dream.
We're probably seeing it as very real and very sort of immutable and very heavy, very weighty.

And one thing about regarding all dharmas as dreams, which I think I may have spoken about sloppily last time, was regarding all dharmas as dreams, regarding reality as a dream does not mean we get to screw around and we don't have to do anything because what the heck, it's just a dream.
Who cares?

Who cares?

That it's our sort of fear and edginess and sort of reactivity to the sort of weighty substance of reality makes it harder for us to really engage in reality.

Familiarization.

Plant a seed and walk away.

It's mysterious.

It's not good.
Creating more suffering.

You know, when there's increased pain and difficulty, we can notice, oh, don't do that.

Aspiration.
